title: Serve vs Own — homepage hero & product copy experiments
content:
Purpose and context:
This working brief pulls together a messaging matrix and draft copy variants intended for homepage and product-page experiments. The framing we want to test: position Redwood as the pragmatic alternative between (a) building and operating inference in-house and (b) handing everything to a black-box API. Many buyer decisions hinge on economics, operational risk, and long-term control — not just raw latency.

Objectives:
- Validate hero-level value props that move mid-market engineering buyers (platform teams, ML infra owners) from curiosity to signup or demo request.
- Create product page lead-ins that answer the top 3 objections: cost predictability, deployment flexibility, and reliability under production load.
- Produce copy for 4 A/B variants to run across hero + top-of-funnel CTA.

Audience segmentation (for copy targeting):
1) Platform teams at scale-ups: care about predictable throughput, SLA, rollout controls.
2) Product engineering (PLG teams): care about fast iteration, simple API, low integration friction.
3) Regulated/enterprise buyers: focus on private deployments, auditability, KMS/HSM, and contractual SLAs.

High-level positioning hypothesis (one sentence):
"Redwood helps teams get production LLM features online with predictable cost, clear deployment choices, and developer ergonomics — without rebuilding inference."

Hero variants (4 distinct angles to test) — short lines + ledes + CTAs
Variant A — Predictable Economics (control-for-cost buyers)
- Hero: "Predictable inference costs, without the guesswork."
- Subhead: "Per-token transparency, autoscaling with cost guards, and batching profiles that cut unit costs in production."
- CTA options: "Estimate your cost" / "See pricing examples"

Variant B — Operational Freedom (control-for-compliance buyers)
- Hero: "Run inference where you need it: cloud, VPC, or on-prem."
- Subhead: "Same API, same toolbelt — pick hosted, dedicated, or fully private deployments with audit-ready controls."
- CTA options: "Compare deployment options" / "Request private demo"

Variant C — Developer Velocity (PLG/product buyers)
- Hero: "Ship LLM features fast — from prototype to scale."
- Subhead: "Streaming responses, function callers, and SDKs that get teams from idea to shipped in hours."
- CTA options: "Get started free" / "Try the quickstart"

Variant D — Resilience & Graceful Degradation (ops-first buyers)
- Hero: "Keep your product online when models or capacity fail."
- Subhead: "Smart routing, fallback model variants, and automatic rollbacks keep SLAs intact under load."
- CTA options: "Request reliability brief" / "See architecture"

Top-page supporting bullets (short, scannable) — unify across variants (pick 3–4):
- "Unified API for hosted, dedicated, and private deployments"
- "Per-route token and latency analytics"
- "Auto-prefix caching and workload-aware batching"
- "Canary rollouts, A/B model routing, and guardrails for regressions"

Product page snippets (targeted for 'Dedicated' and 'Private' pages):
Dedicated (lead):
- Headline: "Reserved GPU pools that behave like a platform"
- Blurb: "Predictable throughput and capacity isolation with configurable autoscale policies. Commit-level pricing for teams that need steady baseline throughput."

Private (lead):
- Headline: "Inference behind your firewall, with Redwood control plane"
- Blurb: "Bring-your-own-network or fully air-gapped options, KMS/HSM integrations, and audit logs for compliance reviews."

Competitive battlecard notes (short):
- Against 'Big cloud managed endpoints' (e.g., vendor X):
  - They win on deep cloud tie-ins and broad managed services; we win on inference-specialized cost controls and model lifecycle primitives tuned for LLMs (KV caching, prefix reuse).
- Against 'LLM API-first providers' (e.g., vendor Y):
  - They win on simplicity and breadth of models; we win on predictable unit economics, deployment flexibility (private/dedicated), and production resilience.
- Against 'Self-hosted open-source runtimes' (teams building their own):
  - They win on perceived control and low run-costs at extreme scale, but lose on maintenance burden, fallback strategies, and observability. Our angle: "Get the economics of ownership without the ops bill."

Key objections to preempt (copy hooks):
- "How much will this cost at scale?" → show worked examples: e.g., 1M tokens/day, common batch profiles, caching assumptions, and effective per-token cost deltas vs naive per-request approaches.
- "We can't send customer data to hosted services." → lead with deploy options and data-in-place guarantees + audit log examples.
- "What happens when a model update breaks quality?" → call out rollouts, eval hooks, and automatic fallbacks.

Proof points / Trust signals to surface:
- SLA language snippets (uptime, p95 latency targets for dedicated)
- Case highlight blurb: "A marketplace platform reduced inference unit cost by 3x using Redwood batching & caching policies" (placeholder customer name to be replaced)
- Performance benchmark callout: "sub-100ms p95 for typical chat flows on dedicated pools (internal results)"

Experiment plan (quick):
- Test matrix: run hero variants A–D across two audience segments: product engineers (top-of-funnel) and platform leads (mid-funnel).
- KPIs: click-through rate on primary CTA, time-to-signup (trial), demo requests, and downstream engagement (API calls in first 7 days).
- Duration: 2 weeks per major variant with ~10k sessions per cell for meaningful CTR signals.
- Secondary: add trust elements (SLA + benchmark + case highlight) to best-performing hero to measure lift on demo requests.

Production notes for handoff to design & analytics:
- Provide 3 visual emphasis levels: (1) pricing-first (charts showing per-token cost), (2) deployment-first (diagram of hosted/dedicated/private toggle), (3) velocity-first (developer SDK flow).
- Analytics: tag CTAs by variant and audience cohort (utm plus cookie) and wire up an early funnel conversion pixel to capture demo requests and trial signups.

Open questions / decisions required:
- Which customer proof can we surface publicly without approvals? (Legal/Customer Success)
- Do we want a dedicated micro-site for "serve vs own" content linking to a deeper technical appendix?
- Which benchmarks are cleared for public use vs internal-only?

Next steps (owner + timeline):
- Aisha: finalize copy choices for A/B and submit to legal by 2026-03-10.
- Marco: wire up analytics tracking and provisional experiment dashboard by 2026-03-17.
- Lina: produce 3 visual sketches and hand off to design by 2026-03-12.

Notes to reviewers: this doc is intentionally practical and experiment-driven; treat claims in the "proof points" section as placeholders until verified by SRE/benchmarks team. Please add any objections you think customers will raise and any direct quotes from sales calls that could be used as micro-copy."
